note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/11 Group 17/11.3 Some reactions of the halide ions.md
outline: Halide ions become stronger reducing agents down Group 17. Aqueous silver ions give AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) and AgI (yellow); ammonia dissolves AgCl when dilute, AgBr when concentrated, but not AgI. Concentrated sulfuric acid first protonates solid halides. Bromide and iodide then reduce the acid: bromide gives bromine and sulfur dioxide, while iodide can give iodine and sulfur dioxide, sulfur or hydrogen sulfide.

misconceptions.statement: Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises chloride to chlorine.

misconceptions.statement: All silver halides dissolve in dilute ammonia.

9701-11.3.1.motivate: Why can iodide turn bromine into bromide, while bromide cannot turn iodine into iodide? The answer is the halide ions' different willingness to give away electrons.
9701-11.3.1.establish: A reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised. The relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents increases down Group 17: $\ce{F- < Cl- < Br- < I-}$. Thus iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide, which is stronger than chloride. In a reaction such as $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$, iodide loses electrons. Consequently iodide can reduce bromine to bromide, but bromide cannot reduce iodine. This reducing trend is the reverse of the oxidising trend of the halogens. Concentrated sulfuric acid illustrates the trend: chloride undergoes only acid-base reaction, bromide also reduces the acid to sulfur dioxide, and iodide can reduce it further, even to hydrogen sulfide.
9701-11.3.1.connect: Use the trend to predict whether a halide will reduce a halogen or concentrated sulfuric acid. Name the halide as the reducing agent when it loses electrons.
9701-11.3.1.note:
- Halide-ion reducing strength: $\ce{F- < Cl- < Br- < I-}$.
- A reducing agent loses electrons and is oxidised.
- Iodide can reduce sulfuric acid more extensively than bromide; chloride does not reduce it.
9701-11.3.1.self_explain: Why does bromide form bromine with concentrated sulfuric acid but chloride does not form chlorine?

9701-11.3.2.motivate: Three colourless halide solutions can be distinguished by the colour of their silver precipitates and their responses to ammonia. A dry salt's reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid gives a second line of evidence.
9701-11.3.2.establish: With aqueous silver ions, $\ce{Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) -> AgX(s)}$. Chloride gives white $\ce{AgCl}$, which dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. Bromide gives cream $\ce{AgBr}$, which dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not dilute ammonia. Iodide gives yellow $\ce{AgI}$, insoluble even in concentrated ammonia. Ammonia lowers the free silver-ion concentration through complex formation, allowing some precipitates to dissolve; the complex formula is not required. Solid halides first undergo acid-base reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid, for example $\ce{NaCl + H2SO4 -> NaHSO4 + HCl}$. Chloride stops there. Bromide also reduces sulfuric acid: $\ce{2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O}$. Iodide produces iodine and can give $\ce{SO2}$, sulfur or $\ce{H2S}$: $\ce{2HI + H2SO4 -> I2 + SO2 + 2H2O}$; $\ce{6HI + H2SO4 -> 3I2 + S + 4H2O}$; $\ce{8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O}$.
9701-11.3.2.connect: The stronger reducing power down Group 17 explains the increasingly extensive reduction of sulfuric acid. The silver test distinguishes the ions through precipitation and ammonia solubility.
9701-11.3.2.note:
- $\ce{AgCl}$ white, dissolves in dilute ammonia.
- $\ce{AgBr}$ cream, dissolves in concentrated ammonia.
- $\ce{AgI}$ yellow, insoluble in ammonia.
- Chloride gives HCl only with concentrated sulfuric acid; bromide and iodide also cause redox.
9701-11.3.2.self_explain: A cream precipitate dissolves only in concentrated ammonia. Which halide ion was present, and how would it react with concentrated sulfuric acid?
